'''Edward Anders''' (June 21, 1926 – June 1, 2025) was a Latvian-born American chemist and professor of chemistry at the [[University of Chicago]]. His major areas of research included the origin and ages of [[meteorites]], the existence of [[presolar grains]] in meteorites, the [[Solar System]] abundance of chemical elements, and mass extinctions in Earth history.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Marvin|first=Ursula B.|title=Oral Histories in Meteoritics and Planetary Sciences: Edward Anders|journal=[[Meteoritics & Planetary Science]]|volume=36|issue=2|pages=A225–A267|date=2001|bibcode=2001M&PSA..36..255M}}</ref> In the 1970s, he was one of the 142 principal investigators who studied lunar samples brought back to Earth by the [[Apollo program]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Compton|first=David W.| url=https://www.hq.nasa.gov/office/pao/History/SP-4214/ch11-4.html|title=Where No Man Has Gone Before: A History of Apollo Lunar Exploration Missions |journal=NASA Special Publication 1214, Chapter 11, Section 4, "The First Lunar Science Conference."|date=1989}}</ref> After retiring from scientific research in 1991, he became a prominent researcher, speaker and writer on issues related to [[the Holocaust]] in Latvia.

== Early life and education ==
Anders was born Edward Alperovitch in the Latvian coastal city of [[Liepāja]] in 1926. Both his mother (Erica, née Sheftelovitch-Meiran) and his father (Adolf) were part of a German-speaking Jewish merchant community. In 1940, the Soviet Union occupied Latvia, and in 1941, Latvia was invaded by Nazi Germany. Anders's father was among many Liepaja Jews murdered by the Nazis in the early months of the occupation. Anders and his mother evaded Nazi annihilation by pretending that she was an Aryan foundling raised by Jews,  until they were able to flee Latvia near the end of World War II.<ref>
{{cite web|last=Goldman|first=Randy M.| url=https://collections.ushmm.org/search/catalog/irn504937|title=Oral History Interview With Edward Anders|publisher=[[U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum]]|volume = RG-50.030.0451|date=February 28, 1997}}</ref>

After the end of the war, Anders settled in Munich, where he attended first the UNRRA University, a makeshift institution created by the [[United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration]] solely to serve refugees, and then the [[Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Holian|first=Anna |title=Displacement and the Post-War Reconstruction of Education: Displaced Persons at the UNRRA University of Munich, 1945-1948 |journal=[[Contemporary European History]]|volume=17|issue=2 |pages=167–195|date=May 2008|jstor=20081400 |doi=10.1017/S0960777308004360 |s2cid=145344395 }}</ref> In August 1948, Anders appeared as a prosecution witness at the Nuremberg [[High Command Trial]], where he gave evidence of German soldiers carrying out lootings and shooting Jewish civilians in Liepaja during 1941.<ref>{{cite court |litigants=United States of America v. Wilhelm von Leeb, et al.|vol=p. 9034-9036 |court=U.S. Military Tribunal, Nuremberg|date=August 2, 1948|}}</ref>

In 1949, Anders arrived in New York City, where he embarked on a master's degree in chemistry at [[Columbia University]]. He earned a Ph.D. from Columbia in 1954, benefiting from the mentorship of Columbia nuclear-chemistry professor Jack Malcolm Miller.<ref>{{cite web | title=Jack Miller Teaching Awards | website=Columbia Chemistry | date=September 9, 2015 | url=https://chem.columbia.edu/department-life/student-awards/jack-miller-teaching-awards/ | access-date=October 20, 2019 | archive-date=October 20, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191020025336/https://chem.columbia.edu/department-life/student-awards/jack-miller-teaching-awards/ | url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Career ==
Anders spent most of his scientific career on the chemistry faculty at the [[University of Chicago]]. He arrived as an assistant professor in 1955, gained tenure a few years later and was named the Horace B. Horton professor in 1973. He spent 1963–64 at the [[University of Bern]] as a visiting professor on sabbatical; he returned to the Swiss university for six shorter stays from 1970 to 1990. His first academic appointment was as an instructor at the [[University of Illinois]] (Champaign-Urbana) from 1954 to 1955.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Marvin|first=Ursula B.| title=Oral Histories in Meteoritics and Planetary Sciences: Edward Anders|journal=[[Meteoritics & Planetary Science]]|volume=36|issue=2|pages=A225–A267|date=2001|bibcode=2001M&PSA..36..255M}}</ref> He received the [[Quantrell Award]].<ref name="Prize">{{cite web|title=Llewellyn John and Harriet Manchester Quantrell Awards for Excellence in Undergraduate Teaching|url=https://www.uchicago.edu/who-we-are/global-impact/accolades/llewellyn-john-and-harriet-manchester-quantrell-awards-for-excellence-in-undergraduate-teaching|website=UChicago}}</ref>

In 1959, Anders won the [[Newcomb Cleveland Prize]] from the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] for his work on meteorites and asteroids.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aaas.org/awards/newcomb-cleveland-prize/recipients|title=Newcomb Cleveland Prize Recipients|website=American Association for the Advancement of Science}}</ref> His findings during this period included evidence that meteorites come from the asteroid belt,<ref>{{cite news|title=History of Meteorites Studied|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1959/10/25/archives/history-of-meteorites-studied.html
|newspaper=New York Times|date=October 25, 1959}}</ref> and an explanation for the ways tiny diamonds could be created in meteorites, without requiring the enormous pressure that could only be found in larger bodies with greater gravitational forces.<ref>{{cite news|last=Sullivan|first=Walter|title=A New Way Found to Make Diamonds|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1961/06/11/archives/a-new-way-found-to-make-diamonds-small-explosion-graphite-and-water.html
|newspaper=New York Times|date=June 11, 1961}}</ref>

In 1973, Anders received the [[NASA Exceptional Scientific Achievement Medal]],<ref name=autogenerated1 /> acknowledging his work analyzing multiple batches of lunar samples brought back to Earth by the Apollo project. In 1974, Britain's [[Royal Astronomical Society]] named him an honorary foreign member, or associate. He also was elected to the U.S. [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1974.<ref>{{cite news|title=Science Academy Elects 96 Members|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1974/04/28/archives/science-academy-elects-96-members.html|newspaper=New York Times|date=April 28, 1974}}</ref>

Anders and colleagues began documenting evidence of stardust within meteorites in 1978, publishing findings in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' suggesting that "primitive meteorites contain yet another kind of alien, presolar material: dust grains ejected from red giants."<ref>B. Srinivasan and E. Anders, ''Science'' '''201''', 51-56 (July 7, 1978)</ref> Subsequent research by Anders and coworkers established the presence of diamonds,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lewis|first1=R.S.|last2=Tang|first2=M.| last3=Wacker|first3=J.F.|last4=Anders|first4=E.|last5=Steel|first5=E.| title=Interstellar Diamonds in Meteorites|journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|volume=326|issue=6109|pages=160–162|date=1987|doi=10.1038/326160a0|bibcode=1987Natur.326..160L|s2cid=4324489}}</ref> silicon carbide and graphite in meteorites' interstellar grains.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Anders|first1=Edward|last2=Zinner|first2=Ernst| title=Interstellar Grains in Primitive Meteorites: Diamond, Silicon Carbide, and Graphite|journal=[[Meteoritics and Planetary Science]]|volume=28|issue=4|pages=490–514|date=1993|bibcode=1993Metic..28..490A|doi=10.1111/j.1945-5100.1993.tb00274.x}}</ref> In a 1991 interview with ''[[Discover (magazine)|Discover]]'', Anders referred to meteorites as "the poor man's space probe."<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Huyghe|first=Patrick|date=November 1991|title=Stardust Memories|magazine=Discover |location=Burbank, California|publisher=Disney Publishing}}</ref>

In the 1980s, Anders and colleagues published evidence in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]''<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Wolbach|first1=Wendy S.|last2=Lewis|first2=Roy S.| last3=Anders|first3=Edward| title=Cretaceous Extinctions: Evidence for Wildfires and Search for Meteoritic Material|journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]]|volume=230|issue=4722|pages=167–170|date=October 11, 1985|doi=10.1126/science.230.4722.167|pmid=17842693|bibcode=1985Sci...230..167W|s2cid=22661861|doi-access=free}}</ref> and ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]''<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Wolbach|first1=Wendy S.|last2=Gilmour|first2=Iain| last3=Anders|first3=Edward|last4=Orth|first4=Charles J.|last5=Brooks|first5=Robert R.| title=Global fire at the Cretaceous-Tertiary Boundary|journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|volume=334|pages=665–669|date=August 1, 1988|issue=6184|doi=10.1038/334665a0|bibcode=1988Natur.334..665W|s2cid=4280587}}</ref> of catastrophic fires 65 million years ago, caused by a giant meteorite crash in the Gulf of Mexico. Their research on the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event]] analyzed silt sediments from sites as far away as Europe and New Zealand. In each case, they found high amounts of iridium (a rare element associated with certain meteorites) and massive amounts of carbon (associated with global fires) in the same layers. "The first year after the impact was a dramatic and dangerous period for life on Earth," Anders told ''[[The New York Times]]''.<ref>{{cite news|title=Global Fire Is Linked to Dinosaur's Demise|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/08/30/science/science-watch-global-fire-is-linked-to-dinosaur-s-demise.|newspaper=New York Times|date=August 30, 1988}}</ref>

In 1989, Anders and Belgian astronomer [[Nicolas Grevesse]] published "Abundances of the Elements,"<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Anders|first1=Edward|last2=Grevasse|first2=Nicolas|title=Abundances of the chemical elements: Meteoritic and solar|journal=[[Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta]]|volume=53|issue=1|pages=197–214|date=January 1989|doi=10.1016/0016-7037(89)90286-X|s2cid=40797942 }}</ref> a scientific paper cataloging the most reliable estimates to date of meteorite and solar abundances of more than 80 elements, ranging from hydrogen to uranium. Their findings have been cited in more than 11,000 subsequent papers by other scientific researchers, according to Google Scholar.<ref>[https://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=7168043835691333135&hl=en&as_sdt=0,5&sciodt=0,5 Google Scholar]</ref>

== Holocaust research ==
In 2003, Anders and co-author Juris Dubrovskis published "Who Died in the Holocaust? Recovering Names From Official Records". Their article, which appeared in [[Holocaust & Genocide Studies]], used Latvian, German, Israeli and other records to document the fate of each of Liepaja's 7,140 Jewish residents during Nazi Germany's occupation. Anders and Dubrovskis established that only 208 survived.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Anders|first1=Edward|last2=Dubrovskis|first2=Juris| url=https://academic.oup.com/hgs/article-abstract/17/1/114/636278|title=Who Died in the Holocaust? Recovering Names From Official Records|journal=[[Holocaust and Genocide Studies]]|volume=17|issue=1|pages=114–138|date=Spring 2003|doi=10.1093/hgs/17.1.114|pmid=20684094|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

In 2004, Latvia's president, [[Vaira Vīķe-Freiberga]], spoke at the dedication of a Holocaust memorial in Liepāja. She closed by saying: "I want to thank the Liepāja Holocaust Memorial Committee, its chairman Mr. Edward Anders, Mr. Vladimirs Bāns, the authors of the project, and all who lent a hand to make this Memorial become reality."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.liepajajews.org/memorial-wall/|title=Memorial Wall – Liepāja Jews in WWII}}</ref>

== Death ==
Anders died in [[San Mateo, California|San Mateo]], [[California]], on June 1, 2025, at the age of 98.<ref>{{cite web | title=Edward Anders, Who Duped Nazis and Illuminated the Cosmos, Dies at 98 | website=[[The New York Times]] | date=19 June 2025 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/19/science/space/edward-anders-dead.html }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=»Im Geiste der Toleranz und des Brückenbaus« – Nachruf auf Edward Anders (in German) |url=https://www.stiftung-denkmal.de/aktuelles/im-geiste-der-toleranz-und-des-brueckenbaus-nachruf-auf-edward-anders-tolerances-un-tiltu-veidosanas-gara-edvarda-andersa-nekrologs/ |access-date=14 June 2025 |publisher=stiftung-denkmal.de |date=2 June 2025}}</ref>
